title: Think Different
tagline: Fired from his own company, he came back and built the most valuable brand in history.

scenes.text: Cupertino, 1997. Apple Computer is 90 days from bankruptcy. Steve Jobs has just returned after twelve years in exile — ousted from the company he founded. He walks back into One Infinite Loop and finds a company making dozens of products, none of them great.

scenes.speaker: Steve Jobs
scenes.text: I asked every person here: which products do we love? Nobody could answer. We make a hundred things and none of them are exceptional. We are going to make four: a desktop for consumers, a desktop for professionals, a laptop for consumers, a laptop for professionals. That is it. Everything else dies.

challenge.instruction: A hundred products, and nobody loves any of them. Sort Apple's line into Jobs's four boxes — consumer or pro — and cut everything else.
challenge.fact: When Jobs returned to Apple in 1997, the company had 350 products. He cut it to 10 — a 2×2 grid of consumer and professional, desktop and portable. 'Deciding what not to do is as important as deciding what to do,' he said. The focus that followed produced the iMac, iPod, iPhone, and iPad within a decade.

scenes.text: In the same year, Jobs launched the 'Think Different' campaign — a tribute to the rebels, misfits, and troublemakers who changed the world. It was not just advertising. It was a statement of identity: Apple exists because the people crazy enough to think they can change the world are the ones who do.

scenes.speaker: Jony Ive
scenes.text: Steve, I've designed something. A computer that comes in five colors, with a translucent shell so you can see the components inside. It looks like it's from the future.

challenge.instruction: Jony Ive's translucent shell lets you see right inside, down to the picture tube. Bend the electron beam with the magnets so it lands on target.
challenge.fact: The iMac went on sale in August 1998 in Bondi Blue, named after the sea at Sydney's Bondi Beach, and became the fastest-selling computer in Apple's history; five fruit colours followed in January 1999.

scenes.speaker: Steve Jobs
scenes.text: The iMac. People are going to think we are insane. They expect a beige box. We are shipping a translucent blue teardrop. Good. Insanity is relative. If we are right about the design, it will change what every computer company makes for the next decade.

challenge.instruction: Under the blue teardrop it still has to work perfectly. Wire the gates so the circuit agrees with the table on every row.
challenge.fact: Jobs insisted that the inside of a machine be as well made as the outside — a lesson, he said, from his father, who finished the backs of cabinets that no one would ever see.

scenes.text: From the iMac to the iPod to the iPhone to the iPad, each product Jobs launched was built on the same conviction: technology and art are not separate things. The device must work perfectly, look perfect, and feel perfect — because the person using it deserves no less. He was right about almost all of it.

challenge.instruction: Technology and art are not separate things — the Mac proved it with letters made of dots. Read the lamps to spell out the campaign that brought Apple back.
challenge.fact: Jobs dropped out of Reed College in 1972 but kept auditing classes — including a calligraphy course by Lloyd Reynolds. That course taught him about serif and sans-serif typefaces, proportional spacing, and typographic beauty. Ten years later, the Macintosh became the first computer with multiple typefaces. 'If I had never dropped in on that course, every Mac would have had the same boring font.'

scenes.speaker: Steve Jobs
scenes.text: I am the most fortunate person I know, because what I loved to do and what the world needed turned out to be the same thing. That almost never happens. If you have that — protect it. Do not let anyone tell you it is not practical. The most practical thing you can do is make something people love.

challenge.instruction: In his years away from Apple, Jobs bet on a small graphics company called Pixar. Balance the Toy Story pipeline so no team holds up the film.
challenge.fact: Jobs' exile produced two revolutions. NeXT's operating system became the foundation of macOS when Apple acquired NeXT in 1997 — bringing Jobs back. Pixar, bought from George Lucas for $10 million in 1986, produced Toy Story (1995), the first fully computer-animated feature film. Disney acquired Pixar for $7.4 billion in 2006, making Jobs Disney's largest individual shareholder.

challenge.instruction: 'Everybody should learn to program a computer, because it teaches you how to think.' Put each program's lines in the right order.
challenge.fact: Steve Jobs said: 'Everybody in this country should learn how to program a computer... because it teaches you how to think.'

challenge.instruction: Today the machines Jobs built change hands for fortunes. Outbid the collectors for the starred relics.
challenge.fact: In 2014 a working Apple-1 — one of about 200 that Jobs and Steve Wozniak built in 1976 — sold at auction in New York for $905,000. Jobs's handwritten 1973 job application has also sold for six figures.

scenes.speaker: Steve Jobs
scenes.text: Diego Maradona and Peter Arnett are still in the rival's hand; they will come to the board one by one. Follow them, start the Business War where they stand, and fight with Kill mode on. A player with no Great People left is out of the game.

challenge.instruction: Fight lesson 7 · Conquest. Deploy, move to wherever the rival stands, start the Business War there, and attack with Kill mode on until the rival has no Great People left.
challenge.fact: With Kill mode on, a beaten card is discarded instead of returning to hand. A player with no Great People left, in hand or on the board, is out, and the last player standing wins. A kill won in a Great Person's own stat also counts towards their achievement.
